citation: Influence of gamified e-learning quizzes on student motivation, SA higher education (SciELO IJTL)
Usage of a mobile social learning platform with virtual badges in a primary school (Computers & Education)
Learner and parent perceptions of visible rewards at two South African high schools (Commonwealth Youth and Development)
M-Thuto: mobile learning for code-switching mathematics learners in SA (SciELO)
mechanisms: Comfort and flexibility at home make online learning feel positive because the learner can control their own schedule, dress, and eating.
The absence of physical presence and structure makes online learning feel isolating and inferior because the learner struggles with self-discipline and misses immediate peer and lecturer feedback.

Interactivity and anonymity in a gamified quiz break monotony and sustain engagement for actively-participating learners, because the learner becomes an active part of the class and learns from seeing others' responses — though the same format risks social loafing or superficial answering for less-engaged learners.
Public leaderboards and real-name displays demotivate participation because the learner evaluates self-worth through social comparison and fears the embarrassment of being seen as the dumbest.

A history of winning or losing shapes whether public reward ceremonies feel fair or exclusionary because the experience of being honoured or left out determines support for visible rewards versus individualised recognition.
objection_patterns: Will I be able to discipline myself without the structure of campus?
Will my wrong answer be displayed publicly and embarrass me?
Will this reward system make me feel excluded if I never win?
Will the teacher give more attention only to award winners?
confidence: Mixed-methods and qualitative, single-province higher education and high school samples, fieldwork around 2021 — mechanisms durable, magnitudes unknown.
